title: The third and fourth weeks
hookLine: walking with Christ through the passion, then the joy of resurrection

cards: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Paul wrote that to the Christians in Rome, about how to treat one another.
The last two weeks of Ignatius of Loyola's Spiritual Exercises ask for something close to it, with one friend at the center.
In the third week, the one praying walks with Jesus through his passion: the supper, the garden, the trial, the cross, the tomb. In the fourth week, through the resurrection and the days after.
Two very different weeks, and one request running through both: to be with him in whatever he's going through.

teach.b: In the third week, Ignatius asks for a grace that can surprise people. Not to explain the cross. Not even, first of all, to feel guilty.
He asks for sorrow with Christ in sorrow: grief, tears, an inner pain at the pain Christ bears for the one praying. It's the prayer of someone sitting beside a friend in a hospital room.
He even suggests noticing how, in the passion, the divinity seems to hide itself and lets the human Jesus suffer terribly.
So the one praying stays near and keeps watch, the way Jesus asked his friends to watch with him in the garden.
In the fourth week, the grace turns over: to be glad and rejoice because of the glory and joy of Christ risen.
John gives that moment one plain sentence: "Then were the disciples glad, when they saw the Lord."
Ignatius also asks the one praying to watch how the risen Christ consoles his friends, the way one friend comforts another. Here's what makes these weeks hard.

teach.h: STEP OUT OF YOUR OWN CENTER.
teach.b: Sorrow and joy on someone else's behalf both mean stepping out of your own center. The fourth week's joy isn't about your own good news. It's gladness that things have gone well for him.
That's an ordinary human skill too, and a tricky one. Crying at a sad film can come easier than being really glad when a friend gets the thing you wanted.
The church calendar keeps both in one shape: Good Friday, and then Easter.

how: In the Spiritual Exercises, the third week contemplates Christ's passion, from the Last Supper to the tomb, and the fourth week his resurrection appearances, ending with the Contemplation to Attain Love.

games.q: what does “the third and fourth weeks” mean?
o: the two weeks of Lent before Easter, kept with fasting and prayer
a two-week silent retreat that closes a monk's first year
the last stages of the Exercises: the passion, then the resurrection

games.q: two weeks, one friend — tap the pairs.
p: seems to hide itself in the passion

s: in the third week, Ignatius mainly asks to understand the cross
he asks for sorrow with Christ in sorrow, the way you'd sit with a friend.
the fourth week's joy is gladness for Christ, not for yourself
Ignatius asks to rejoice because of the glory and joy of Christ risen.
John says the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord
"then were the disciples glad, when they saw the Lord."

games.q: a friend is going through the worst week of their life. what does the third week's grace look like?
o: stay near and share the sorrow.
change the subject to cheer them up.
games.why: Ignatius asks for sorrow with Christ in sorrow: staying near and keeping watch, the way Jesus asked his friends to watch with him in the garden.

practice: First stay a while near the cross, or near someone you know who is suffering right now, without trying to fix anything.

Then turn: go to the garden on the first morning, or bring to mind someone whose life just went well, and let any gladness be for them, not for you. If you pray, hold both before God; if not, notice how each one sits in your body.

wordCard.voice: The third and fourth weeks. The passion, then the resurrection, prayed as a friend: sorrow with Christ in sorrow, and joy with Christ in joy.

carryVoice: Your line: with him in both. Sorrow and gladness, both on someone else's behalf. Back tomorrow, same hill.
